newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Oil prices surge, stocks fall in Asia on Iraq raid.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices surge, stocks fall in Asia on Iraq raid.

text.p: News that the U.S. had attacked military targets in Iraq swept through Asian financial markets on Tuesday, with the most dramatic and immediate impact seen in oil prices which rose sharply.
Share prices fell strongly in most centres, while the dollar strengthened and gold inched higher.

In Singapore, North Sea Brent crude oil futures briefly hit their highest level since the 1990-91 Gulf War. October Brent surged to $23.50 a barrel, up $1.51 from Monday's London close, after news of the U.S. attack but slid back to $22.45 in late trade.

In Tokyo, a senior economist at the Japanese Institute of Middle Eastern Economies, Kazuaki Kondo, predicted the price of light crude oil traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange-- another key price barometer-- could soar to $30 if hostilities escalated.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index dropped sharply in response to the news of the raid, ending 1.35 percent down at 10,957.18. Market sentiment was already low because of fears of higher interest rates.

Turnover reached HK$800 million (US$103 million) during the first 15 minutes of afternoon trade after Washington said it had attacked Iraq, Alan Hutcheson, director of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said.
The Pentagon said the U.S. military launched cruise missile strikes against targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds in the north of the country.

Iraqi President Saddam Hussein responded in a defiant speech by urging his air force and anti-aircraft gunners to attack U.S. and allied planes policing Western-imposed air exclusion zones in the south and north of his country.

Anthony Edwards, a director at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in Hong Kong, said traders must remain cautious because of the potential impact on commodities markets if the situation became protracted. "Then that is a concern," he said.
Michael Hung, research manager of Nikko Securities in Taiwan said he expected the market to fall further on Wednesday after Tuesday's 1.33 percent drop to 6,257.97 points.
"What worries people most is the potential rises in domestic oil prices and inflation," he said.

Thai stocks fell sharply in what dealers described as panicked selling, with the key index tumbling 48.45 points to hit an intraday low of 1,037.78 points. It recovered to end the session down 2.01 percent at 1,064.45 points.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who is campaigning for re-election, was due to make a statement on the retaliatory strike against Iraq at about 1200 GMT.
News of the attacks came just as Tokyo's Nikkei 225-share index ended with a modest gain. The index closed up 91.04 points to 20,198.15.
"The market could not digest the news before the close," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy manager of Nomura Securities Co.
Before reports of the missile strikes, market sentiment was dominated by Wall Street's decline last week on fears of higher U.S. interest rates.
Concern over rates had intensified because of a report in Tuesday's Wall Street Journal.
The report said the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates by half a percentage point, twice what markets now expect, if forthcoming economic data suggested the economy was overheating.
U.S. markets were closed on Monday for the Labor Day holiday.
Talk of higher interest rates, combined with the U.S. raid, pushed the dollar to a high of 109.35 yen in Tokyo, before it eased to 109.25 against 109.16 in Europe overnight.
By 1150 GMT, the dollar was trading at 109.29/39 yen and 1.4865/70 marks.
The price of gold in Hong Kong firmed minutes after the strikes were launched and ended the day at US$387.20/387.70 an ounce, up from US$386.70/387.20 earlier.
